content: The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that less than 1% of individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART) globally are using third-line regimens. However, the demand for these regimens is expected to rise as access to viral load monitoring and the use of firstand second-line ART continues to expand. Third-line drugs are often more expensive than firstand second-line options, or their costs remain undefined, which may hinder their adoption in resource-limited settings. While developing policies to improve access to third-line ART is important, it should not compromise the availability of firstand second-line treatments. There is limited research on the use of newer antiretroviral (ARV) drugs in third-line regimens for children, adolescents, and pregnant or breastfeeding women. Data on pharmacokinetics and safety in these populations are particularly scarce. Consequently, strategies to balance the benefits and risks of third-line treatments must be explored when second-line therapy fails. A systematic review and network meta-analysis have shown that newer drugs generally exhibit good efficacy and tolerability in treatment-experienced patients. However, no direct comparisons have been conducted to determine the clinical advantages of one drug over another. Based on the available evidence, darunavir (DRV) and dolutegravir (DTG) are recommended for use in third-line regimens for children. There is uncertainty about whether these drugs should be used in combination or as part of a standard nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI)-backbone regimen. Darunavir cannot be used in children under three years of age and is only available as a single drug through a donation program in select countries. Additionally, no pediatric fixed-dose combination (FDC) of DRV with ritonavir (RTV) is currently available. Dolutegravir is approved for adolescents aged 12 years and older, but its availability is expected to remain limited. A safety and dose-finding trial (IMPAACT 1093) is underway, with completion expected to support pediatric registration by stringent regulatory agencies. For children with no new ARV options after second-line regimen failure, continuing a tolerated regimen is recommended. If ART is discontinued, attention should be given to preventing opportunistic infections, symptom relief, and pain management. There is also limited data on the use of newer third-line drugs in pregnant or breastfeeding women. Animal studies have not indicated fetal toxicity with INSTIs, but in the absence of well-controlled studies in pregnant women and pharmacokinetic data to guide dosing during pregnancy, dolutegravir should only be used during pregnancy if clearly indicated. Further research is urgently needed to guide third-line ART strategies in resource-limited settings. Priorities include monitoring critical outcomes for individuals on second-line ART, exploring once-daily dosing for DRV/r and raltegravir (RAL) as alternatives to NRTI-based regimens in second-line therapy, developing heat-stable formulations of DRV/r, and evaluating the pharmacokinetics, safety, and efficacy of new drugs in children, adolescents, and pregnant women. Assessing the pharmacokinetics and safety of dolutegravir in pregnant women is particularly urgent. Pharmacovigilance research is also needed, including studies on the long-term safety of and potential interactions with drugs used for tuberculosis, malaria, hepatitis, and opioid substitution therapy. As the HIV epidemic evolves in resource-limited settings, pilot studies on implementing third-line ART in low-resource environments are critically needed.
